chapters.file: ch15 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
chapters.relation: Kroustallis reads Lust, Caution through perception rather than hidden emotion, arguing Wong Chia Chi abandons the disengaged, sight-only aesthetic of Mrs. Mak and comes to perceive Mr. Yee's world with her whole engaged body. He uses Merleau-Ponty's Phenomenology of Perception to justify the three graphic sex scenes as bodily, essentially ambiguous cognition (the lipstick-marked cup, the flat key as motor intentionality) that links perception directly to action without unconscious representations. He frames Wong's development toward harmony via Fang Dongmei's neo-Confucian 'creative creativity' and a yin-yang polarity of meek and strong, with rain and jasmine flowers as an engaged natural environment.

chapters.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
ch17 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
chapters.relation: Barkman argues Lee's Hulk is a parable about lost Paradise and a polemic against materialist reductionism of human nature. The villains David Banner and Talbot are metaphysical materialists (and social Darwinists) who reduce Bruce to DNA to be exploited, while Bruce and Betty treat human nature as an immaterial, indivisible soul with nondegreed essential capacities for rationality, language and morality. Drawing on an Aristotelian/Judeo-Christian view of substance and soul, he reads Lee's CGI mapping of Bana's eyes onto the green body as showing Bruce and the Hulk are one ensouled person, and Bruce's Golden Gate and dog-attack rescues as the soul actualizing its capacity to act morally.

chapters.file: ch18 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
chapters.relation: Dale and Foy argue that across Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, Hulk and Brokeback Mountain, Lee presents a pessimistic, Sartrean philosophy of identity in which authentic selves are irreconcilable with a hostile social world. They read Jen's caged gender rebellion and Jade Fox's rejection, Bruce's suppressed origins and rage-fueled transformation, and Ennis and Jack's concealed love as hidden identities that produce dislocation, deception and disorder. Invoking Kierkegaard and Heidegger's dasein on authenticity and Foucault's Discipline and Punish, they show society disciplining deviance so each hero is displaced or destroyed—Jack beaten to death like Matthew Shepard, the Hulk exiled to the Amazon.

chapters.file: ch19 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
chapters.relation: Zietsma reads Hulk and Taking Woodstock as antiwar films that subvert the hegemonic culture of heroic violence, fitting Lackey's category of universal (Gandhian/early-Christian) pacifism. He argues both films disturb their genre's expected narrative and demasculinize the hero: Elliot the gay nonviolent hero and the transgender vet Vilma, and a weeping Hulk who is rescued by Betty and finally gives up his power rather than kill David Banner. He reads the bathroom-mirror 'Puny human' scene as an inverted Lacanian mirror stage unmasking America's violent militarism, framing the Vietnam War and war on terror as violence that only begets more violence.

chapters.file: ch20 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
chapters.relation: Kang argues Lee's Taking Woodstock desexualizes and 'recloset[s]' Elliot Tiber's gay coming-out memoir, substituting a fluid 'queer' openness for Tiber's political gay identity and framing his homosexuality as an incidental, situationally-straight product of the festival (the woman-centered threesome, the chaste kiss with Paul). Drawing on Sedgwick, Butler and Foucault's history of sexuality, she critiques how the film neutralizes homophobia and omits the gay Buddhist mentor Georgette, whose teaching on karma, samsara and dukkha grounds Tiber's self-acceptance and unconditional love—reducing a gay everyman's struggle to one 'not-normal freak' among a hundred thousand.

chapters.file: ch21 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
chapters.relation: Schmetkamp reads The Ice Storm through the philosophy of love and Hegelian recognition theory, defending a dialogical model of love (Krebs, Scheler's shared feeling) against union (Plato, Nozick, Solomon) and care (Aristotle, Frankfurt) models. She shows the Hood and Carver families lack autonomy-granting mutual recognition: Ben and Janey's affair is mere egoistic gratification, Elena would surrender her 'I' for a 'we', and Mikey seeks stilled 'molecules' and the Fantastic Four's negative zone. Invoking Sartre's the-look as objectification and shame, she argues Mikey's death finally breaks the ice through empathy and sympathy (Scheler, Stein), as Jim weeps and Elena speaks Ben's name.

chapters.file: ch22 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
chapters.relation: Koepsell reads The Ice Storm as an existentialist masterpiece dramatizing Sartre's Being and Nothingness in Nixon's America. He maps Paul's Fantastic Four 'negative space/void' monologue onto Sartrean no-thing-ness and the tension between being-in-itself, being-for-itself and being-for-others, arguing the alienated, bourgeois Hoods and Carvers live inauthentically in bad faith, objectifying one another. Mikey's joyous reveling in the ice storm before his electrocution is a fleeting authentic immersion in existence (like Roquentin in Nausea), and the closing embraces—Wendy hugging Sandy, a weeping Ben meeting Paul—show characters momentarily overcoming alienation and freely remaking their essence.

chapters.file: ch23 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
chapters.relation: Hole reads The Ice Storm's prophetic opening as a meditation on 'what is impending', weaving existentialism with Zen Buddhism and Daoism. He uses the Four Noble Truths and the Zen story of the monk 'still carrying the woman' to show the families suffer through attachment to rigid self-images, and Jung's synchronicity and the Daoist dao/wu-wei to read the ice storm's formation and Mikey's chance electrocution as an interdependent flow the characters resist. Centrally he applies Heidegger's being-toward-death—death as ownmost, non-relational, not-to-be-outstripped—arguing that fleeing one's death is fleeing one's authentic being, alongside Kierkegaard's leap of faith and Nietzsche's living dangerously; he closes by applying the argument to his own mortality.

chapters.file: ch24 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee.md
chapters.relation: Mahon asks whether Ride with the Devil endorses the proverb that all's fair in love and war, locating the film's moral core in its outsiders—the German immigrant Jake, the freed slave Holt, and the young widow Sue Lee. Against Sunzi's undiscriminating claim that warfare is the art of deceit, he argues the film sides with Machiavelli's Discourses distinction between honorable ruses of war and dishonorable perfidy: the bushwhackers' wearing of Union blue and Jake's lies are ruses, but the Lawrence massacre and refusing to ambush women under a truce mark limits Jake will not cross. In love, Sue Lee's shift from romantic lying to 'now is the truth' shows honesty is finally required, so all is not fair.

holes.name: Fang Dongmei (Thomé H. Fang)
holes.what: Twentieth-century Taiwanese neo-Confucian philosopher who synthesized Confucianism, Daoism and Whiteheadian/Bergsonian process thought into a metaphysics of 'comprehensive harmony' and 'creative creativity'.
holes.why: Chapter 15 leans heavily on Fang Dongmei's 'creative creativity' and comprehensive-harmony scheme to explain Wong Chia Chi's moral development, and no taxonomy philosopher covers this figure.

holes.name: Arnold Berleant
holes.what: Contemporary American aesthetician who founded environmental aesthetics on engaged, participatory sensory 'aisthesis', rejecting the disengaged-observer paradigm of fine-art appreciation.
holes.why: Chapter 15's whole first movement applies Berleant's engaged environmental aesthetics to Wong's shift from sight-only performer to whole-body participant, and the taxonomy has no philosopher or concept for it.

holes.name: Pacifism (universal / antiwar pacifism)
holes.what: The ethical position, with variants from universal (all violence is destructive) to antiwar pacifism (self-defense permitted, war not), that violence should be renounced as a path to redemption.
holes.why: Chapter 19's core thesis classifies Hulk and Taking Woodstock as Lackey's 'universal pacifism' and argues nonviolence is the only redemption; the taxonomy has ahimsa and just-war-theory but no general pacifism concept.
